airport: large airport facilities with broad paved aviation areas and terminal-like structures, distinguishing airport from parking by lacking organized parked-vehicle rows, from resort by lacking leisure-oriented open-space layout, and from port by lacking shoreline docks and harbor-water context.
bareland: broad exposed ground with barren surface and little vegetation, distinguishing bareland from desert by showing less homogeneous sand texture, from playground by lacking sports-ground organization, and from meadow by lacking grass-dominant natural vegetation texture.
baseballfield: compact sports field with a clear baseball-diamond layout and central infield geometry, distinguishing baseballfield from playground by stronger game-field structure and from meadow by lacking broad natural grassland texture.
beach: bright shoreline region with clear sand-water boundary and coastal texture, distinguishing beach from resort by weaker built leisure infrastructure, from pond by broader shoreline scale, and from desert by direct water contact.
bridge: narrow man-made crossing structure spanning water or land, distinguishing bridge from viaduct by its more localized crossing form, from pond by being a crossing rather than a compact water body, and from industrial by lacking factory-like compounds.
center: dense urban core with concentrated buildings and organized city-block layout, distinguishing center from stadium by lacking a dominant sports field, from square by broader surrounding built-up structure, and from church by lacking a single landmark-like religious complex.
church: prominent religious building or complex with distinctive landmark-like architecture, distinguishing church from square by stronger building dominance, from center by emphasizing a single landmark structure rather than a broad urban core, and from denseresidential by lacking repeated neighborhood housing patterns.
commercial: organized business district with dense building blocks and road access, distinguishing commercial from square by stronger building dominance, from industrial by lacking heavy factory compounds, and from parking by having dense structures rather than open paved vehicle space.
denseresidential: tightly packed residential roofs with very high housing density and minimal spacing, distinguishing denseresidential from mediumresidential by much closer building intervals, from sparseresidential by a far denser neighborhood texture, and from industrial by smaller repeated housing roofs rather than factory-like compounds.
desert: wide dry barren region with homogeneous arid texture and very little vegetation, distinguishing desert from pond by lacking water, from bareland by stronger sand-like continuity, and from mountain by weaker terrain relief.
farmland: regular cultivated land with visible parcel boundaries and agricultural texture, distinguishing farmland from meadow by stronger man-made plot organization, from industrial by lacking factory compounds and storage yards, and from airport by lacking aviation pavement and terminal structures.
forest: dense continuous tree canopy with natural dark-green texture, distinguishing forest from mountain by weaker relief, from pond by lacking a central water body, and from meadow by denser canopy continuity.
industrial: large factory-like compounds with utilitarian building layouts, storage yards, and production infrastructure, distinguishing industrial from storagetanks by not being dominated only by circular tank clusters, from railwaystation by weaker rail-line concentration, and from denseresidential by larger production-oriented structures rather than repeated residential roofs.
meadow: broad natural grass-covered open area with soft vegetation texture and weak structural boundaries, distinguishing meadow from farmland by lacking regular parcel boundaries, from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant, and from forest by lacking dense continuous canopy.
mediumresidential: moderately spaced residential houses with visible yards and balanced housing density, distinguishing mediumresidential from sparseresidential by denser neighborhood grouping, from denseresidential by larger spacing between buildings, and from resort by showing a more regular residential layout rather than leisure-oriented organization.
mountain: rugged elevated terrain with strong relief, slope shadows, and irregular topographic texture, distinguishing mountain from forest by more obvious terrain variation, from pond by lacking a compact water body, and from desert by stronger relief and slope structure.
park: planned green open space with vegetation, paths, and leisure-oriented layout, distinguishing park from square by stronger vegetation presence, from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant, and from playground by weaker explicit sports-ground structure.
parking: large open paved area with organized parking rows and vehicle-oriented layout, distinguishing parking from airport by lacking runways and aviation facilities, from viaduct by lacking elevated crossing structure, and from port by lacking dock-water harbor context.
playground: recreational activity area with sports or play surfaces and open activity layout, distinguishing playground from baseballfield by lacking a baseball-diamond infield, from stadium by weaker enclosure and spectator structure, and from park by showing more explicit play-ground geometry.
pond: small enclosed water body with compact shape and visible boundary, distinguishing pond from river by lacking a long continuous winding channel, from forest by clear water dominance, and from park by being water-dominant rather than vegetation-dominant.
port: waterfront transport area with docks, vessels, and harbor-side logistics infrastructure, distinguishing port from resort by stronger transport and dock organization, from airport by the presence of shoreline-water context, and from parking by lacking a purely inland open vehicle layout.
railwaystation: transport hub with concentrated rail lines and station-related structures, distinguishing railwaystation from viaduct by stronger station-node and rail-line concentration, from industrial by clearer transport-line organization, and from airport by lacking long aviation runways.
resort: leisure-oriented built environment with organized open spaces and accommodation-like structures, distinguishing resort from port by weaker dock-industrial structure, from beach by stronger built tourism layout, and from sparseresidential by a more leisure-oriented spatial organization rather than repeated housing plots.
river: elongated natural watercourse with continuous winding channel and visible banks, distinguishing river from pond by its longer linear flow shape, from bridge by being a natural channel rather than a crossing structure, and from forest by clear water appearance.
school: campus-like area with multiple institutional buildings, open grounds, and organized educational layout, distinguishing school from square by stronger campus structure, from resort by weaker leisure-oriented organization, and from park by more institutional building presence.
sparseresidential: widely separated residential houses with large open gaps and low housing density, distinguishing sparseresidential from mediumresidential by much larger spacing, from denseresidential by far lower roof density, and from resort by more regular residential neighborhood structure.
square: open civic plaza-like space embedded in urban area, distinguishing square from church by weaker landmark-building dominance, from park by less vegetation, and from commercial by more central open-space structure and less dense building coverage.
stadium: large sports complex with prominent field and stronger enclosure or spectator-related structure, distinguishing stadium from playground by more venue-like framing, from center by emphasizing a dedicated sports facility, and from park by stronger field-centered sports organization.
storagetanks: clusters of large circular industrial tanks with highly regular round geometry, distinguishing storagetanks from industrial by stronger circular-container dominance, from pond by lacking natural water texture, and from port by weaker harbor-water context.
viaduct: elongated elevated transport structure with clear grade-separated roadway form, distinguishing viaduct from bridge by its more extended raised-traffic pattern, from railwaystation by lacking concentrated station-like rail organization, and from parking by lacking flat vehicle rows.
